title: Langevin Autoencoders for Learning Deep Latent Variable Models

en.text: Train a deep latent variable model (DLVM) by maximum likelihood and you immediately hit the same wall everyone hits: the objective contains an expectation over the posterior p(z|x), and that posterior almost never has a closed form. How you approximate it has, for years, split deep generative modeling into two camps.

The first camp is variational inference (VI) — the machinery behind the VAE. An encoder network predicts the latents for every data point in a single forward pass, and that amortization is what makes training fast. The price is expressiveness: the encoder can only emit a tractable distribution, usually a Gaussian, so the quality of the approximation is capped by that family no matter how much you train. The second camp is Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC), and Langevin dynamics in particular. MCMC samples from the true posterior without assuming its shape, so it can be arbitrarily flexible. Its problem has always been speed: the textbook version runs a separate sampling chain for every single data point, and it converges slowly, which is why it has rarely been practical for training deep models.

This NeurIPS 2022 paper from the University of Tokyo asks whether you can have both — the amortized efficiency of VI and the sampling flexibility of MCMC. Its answer is the Langevin Autoencoder (LAE), built on a new sampling algorithm the authors call Amortized Langevin Dynamics (ALD). The one-line intuition: take the noise that Langevin sampling injects into the latent variables, and move it onto the encoder's parameters instead.

en.caption: Figure 1. Four ways to approximate the posterior. (a) Variational inference fits a tractable family such as a Gaussian; (b) traditional Langevin dynamics runs gradient-based sampling iterations directly on the latents, per data point; (c) Hoffman [2017] uses an encoder to initialize those Langevin chains but still iterates per data point; (d) ALD also uses an encoder, but treats its output directly as a posterior sample and performs the update implicitly by updating the encoder's parameters.

· Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.07036
· Code: https://github.com/iShohei220/LAE
The problem: MCMC is more accurate, so why doesn't anyone train with it?

Start with the tension. Gradient-based maximum-likelihood learning needs an expectation over p(z|x), and that posterior has no closed form. VI answers this by fitting a tractable stand-in distribution: one encoder pass yields latents for the whole dataset, but the stand-in's shape is fixed in advance — a Gaussian stays a Gaussian, and it struggles the moment the true posterior is multimodal or strongly correlated.

MCMC takes the opposite route. It assumes nothing about the posterior's shape and samples from it directly, so in principle it can approximate an arbitrarily complex posterior. Langevin dynamics is one such method: it follows the gradient of the log-posterior and adds a dose of Gaussian noise, nudging samples toward high-probability regions step by step. The catch is its per-datapoint nature — every new observation needs its own full sampling chain, and with thousands of training points that cost is prohibitive. Hybrids like Hoffman [2017] use an encoder to give each chain a better starting point, but the sampling iterations themselves are still run per data point, a cost paid at both training and test time.
The method: let the Langevin noise act on the encoder's parameters

The key move in ALD is to change what the randomness acts on. Traditional Langevin runs a stochastic differential equation (SDE) on each latent z; ALD instead defines a deterministic encoder f(x; φ) that maps observations to latents, and runs the Langevin equation on the encoder's parameters φ. Because the latents are produced by the encoder, dynamics on φ induce dynamics on the latent space — so the encoder's outputs can be read off directly as posterior samples.

Written out, the update on the parameters is dφ = −∇φ V(φ) dt + √2 dB, where the potential V(φ) = Σ U(x⁽ⁱ⁾, f(x⁽ⁱ⁾; φ); θ) sums the negative log-joint over all data points. Discretized, each step is a draw from a Gaussian: φ′ ~ N(φ − η∇φV(φ), 2ηI). The important detail is that every data point shares the same parameters φ, so a single update advances the sampling for all of them at once — which is exactly what amortization means here.

Moving the noise onto the parameters isn't free, though: you need a guarantee that the latents you read off are actually distributed according to the posterior you wanted. The paper's Theorem 1 supplies the condition. When the encoder has the form f(x; Φ) = Φ g(x) — a fixed feature extractor g followed by a trainable last linear layer Φ — and the width d of that layer is at least the number of data points n in the batch, the latent samples induced by ALD converge to the true posterior. Two clean special cases fall out: traditional Langevin dynamics is a special case of ALD, and the ordinary autoencoder is a special case of the LAE.

The Langevin Autoencoder simply folds this sampler into the training loop. Before each decoder update, it runs T ALD steps on the encoder's last layer to draw posterior samples, optionally followed by a Metropolis-Hastings (MH) rejection step that removes the bias introduced by discretization. In code it looks almost identical to a standard autoencoder — the only difference is that the encoder takes a few noisy update steps along the way.
That d ≥ n condition is not just theory. In a bivariate-Gaussian toy problem, the authors vary the input dimensionality d of the encoder's last layer and watch what happens to the samples.

en.caption: Figure 2. Effect of encoder capacity in the bivariate-Gaussian toy example; d is the input dimensionality of the encoder's last linear layer. When d > n and d = n, the samples for all three data points cover their true posteriors (GT); once d < n, the middle data point's samples collapse to a single point — a direct confirmation of the rank condition d ≥ n in Theorem 1.

en.text: Evidence I: ALD reaches posteriors that VI cannot

Where does the flexibility actually show up? The paper uses a "neural likelihood" toy example: the likelihood is defined by a randomly initialized neural network, engineering a posterior that is both multimodal and strongly correlated, and then asks which methods can recover it. Shapes like this are precisely where a Gaussian stand-in breaks down.

en.caption: Figure 3. Posterior comparison on the neural-likelihood example. From left to right: the ground-truth posterior (GT), mean-field VI, full VI, and samples from ALD. Mean-field VI captures only one mode, full VI manages a single correlated ellipse, while ALD's samples reproduce the multimodal, curved structure of the true posterior.

en.text: The read is straightforward. Mean-field VI collapses the whole posterior into one isolated mode; full VI does a little better but still amounts to a single tilted ellipse — both discard the true multimodal, curved structure. ALD's samples, by contrast, trace the actual shape. That is the flexibility of genuine MCMC coming back into a setting where the variational family simply could not reach.
Evidence II: a more accurate posterior buys a better generative model

The toy example shows ALD samples accurately, but does that accuracy pay off when training a real deep generative model? The paper runs image generation on four standard datasets — MNIST, SVHN, CIFAR-10, and CelebA. For a fair comparison every method uses the same fully-connected networks, and quality is measured by the negative ELBO (evidence lower bound) per dimension, averaged over three seeds; lower is better.

en.caption: Table 1. Image-generation results on four datasets, measured by negative ELBO per dimension (mean over three seeds, lower is better). LAE achieves the lowest value on all four datasets, consistently ahead of the VAE, VAE-flow, and Hoffman [2017].

en.text: LAE posts the lowest negative ELBO on all four: MNIST drops from the VAE's 1.189 to 1.177, CIFAR-10 from 4.820 to 4.773, CelebA from 4.671 to 4.636, and SVHN from 4.442 to 4.412. The absolute gains are modest, but the direction is consistent — more accurate posterior sampling does translate into a better-trained generative model. The cost is wall-clock: LAE trains about 2.24× slower than a plain VAE, though it runs at essentially the same speed as the sampling-based Hoffman [2017] baseline. And all of this uses just T = 2 ALD iterations.
What's doing the work: the MH step and the iteration count T
If T = 2 is enough, how much does T matter at all — and is the MH rejection step worth its cost? The paper answers with learning curves of the negative ELBO on MNIST's test set.

en.caption: Figure 4. Learning curves of the negative ELBO on MNIST's test set. The T = 2 and T = 10 curves nearly coincide, so beyond two steps more ALD iterations barely help; dropping the MH rejection step (No MH steps) makes the curve oscillate wildly, showing that the MH step is important for stabilizing training.

en.text: Two things stand out. First, the T = 2 and T = 10 curves sit almost on top of each other, so once ALD runs at least two steps, adding more brings little — which is why the image experiments use only T = 2. Second, remove the MH rejection step and the curve starts swinging violently; training visibly destabilizes. The MH step costs a bit of extra computation but is what keeps training stable. Together with Figure 2, these two ablations pin down the method's behavior from both ends — the theoretical condition (d ≥ n) and the engineering details (MH, T).
Takeaway: the autoencoder, reread as a bias-corrected sampler

The most elegant thing about this work is the rearrangement of where the randomness lives. Move the Langevin noise from the latents to the encoder's parameters, and sampling becomes both efficient — because it is amortized across all the data — and flexible — because it is genuine MCMC rather than a constrained Gaussian. The resulting LAE is a provably valid MCMC method, looks almost exactly like a standard autoencoder in code, and still beats the VAE on test likelihood.

Seen from another angle, it reframes the familiar autoencoder as a sampling-based, bias-corrected alternative to variational inference. The boundaries are worth stating plainly: the convergence guarantee relies on a specific encoder structure — a fixed feature extractor with a trainable linear last layer and d ≥ n — the experiments center on fully-connected networks and these standard datasets, the absolute gains are gentle, and you pay roughly 2.24× the training time. It reads less as a finished replacement and more as an opened door: MCMC, for the first time, genuinely amortized into the training of deep generative models.

zh.text: 训练一个深度隐变量模型（deep latent variable model，DLVM），最直接的想法是最大化数据的似然。但只要模型里有隐变量 z，这个目标就绕不开一个对后验分布 p(z|x) 的期望，而这个后验通常没有闭式解，必须逐点做蒙特卡洛估计。围绕“如何近似这个后验”，深度生成模型这些年基本分成了两条路。

第一条路是变分推断（variational inference，VI），也就是我们熟悉的 VAE。它用一个编码器网络一次性为所有数据点预测隐变量，这种“摊销（amortization）”让训练变得非常高效。代价是：编码器只能输出一个可解析的分布（通常是高斯），所以它的近似能力天然被这个分布族卡住了。第二条路是马尔可夫链蒙特卡洛（MCMC），尤其是 Langevin 动力学。它能精确地从复杂后验里采样，但一直有个老问题：慢。传统做法要为每一个数据点单独跑一条采样链，而且收敛不快，因此几乎没法用来训练深度模型。

这篇来自东京大学、发表于 NeurIPS 2022 的工作想问的是：能不能把 VI 的“摊销效率”和 MCMC 的“采样灵活性”合到一起？他们给出的答案是 Langevin 自编码器（Langevin Autoencoder，LAE），核心是一个叫“摊销 Langevin 动力学（Amortized Langevin Dynamics，ALD）”的新采样算法。一句话概括：把 Langevin 采样里的随机噪声，从隐变量空间搬到编码器的参数上。

zh.caption: 图1 四种后验近似方法的对比。(a) 变分推断用高斯等可解析分布去逼近后验；(b) 传统 Langevin 动力学直接在隐变量上逐点跑采样迭代；(c) Hoffman [2017] 用编码器为传统 Langevin 采样提供初始点，但仍然要逐点迭代；(d) 本文的 ALD 同样用编码器，但直接把编码器的输出当作后验样本，采样过程通过更新编码器参数隐式完成。

zh.text: 论文与代码链接：
· 论文：https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.07036
· 代码：https://github.com/iShohei220/LAE
问题：MCMC 明明更准，为什么没人拿它训练
先把矛盾摆清楚。基于梯度的最大似然学习，需要对后验 p(z|x) 求一个期望，而这个后验没有闭式表达。VI 的解法是找一个可解析的替身分布去逼近它，好处是编码器一次前向就能给出所有数据点的隐变量，坏处是替身分布的形状被写死了——高斯就是高斯，遇到多峰或强相关的后验只能勉强拟合。

MCMC 走的是另一条路：不假设后验长什么样，而是直接从中采样，因此原则上能逼近任意复杂的后验。Langevin 动力学是其中一种，它沿着对数后验的梯度走、再叠加一点高斯噪声，逐步把样本推向高概率区域。问题在于它的“逐点”本性：每来一个数据点，就要为它单独跑一整条采样链，训练时数据点成千上万，成本无法接受。已有的折中方案（如 Hoffman [2017]）用编码器给采样链提供一个更好的起点，但采样迭代本身还是逐点进行的，训练和测试时都要付这份钱。
方法：让 Langevin 噪声作用在编码器参数上
ALD 的关键一步，是换一个施加随机性的对象。传统 Langevin 把随机微分方程（SDE）跑在每个隐变量 z 上；ALD 则定义一个确定性的编码器 f(x; φ)，把数据映射到隐变量，然后把 Langevin 方程跑在编码器的参数 φ 上。因为隐变量是编码器算出来的，参数 φ 的动力学就会诱导出隐变量空间上的动力学，于是可以直接把编码器的输出当作后验样本。
参数上的 Langevin 更新写出来是这样：dφ = −∇φ V(φ) dt + √2 dB，其中势能 V(φ) = Σ U(x⁽ⁱ⁾, f(x⁽ⁱ⁾; φ); θ) 把所有数据点的负对数联合概率加在一起。离散化后每一步就是从一个高斯里采样：φ′ ~ N(φ − η∇φV(φ), 2ηI)。注意这里所有数据点共享同一组参数 φ，一次更新就同时推进了全部数据点的采样——这正是“摊销”的含义。

但把噪声搬到参数上不会白搬，需要一个保证：这样采出来的隐变量，真的服从我们想要的后验吗？论文的 Theorem 1 给出了条件。当编码器写成 f(x; Φ) = Φ g(x)，即一个固定的特征提取器 g 后面接一个可训练的最后一层线性映射 Φ，并且这个线性层的维度 d 不小于当前 batch 的数据点数 n 时，ALD 诱导出的隐变量样本会收敛到真实后验。两个漂亮的特例随之而来：传统 Langevin 动力学是 ALD 的特例，而普通的自编码器则是 LAE 的特例。
Langevin 自编码器（LAE）就是把这套采样直接嵌进训练循环：每次更新解码器参数之前，先在编码器最后一层上跑 T 步 ALD 得到后验样本，可选地再加一个 Metropolis-Hastings（MH）拒绝步来消除离散化带来的偏差。从代码上看，它和一个标准自编码器几乎一模一样，区别只是编码器多走了几步带噪声的更新。
这个 d ≥ n 的条件不是纸上谈兵。下图在一个二元高斯的玩具例子上，直接改变编码器最后一层的输入维度 d，观察采样结果。

zh.caption: 图2 编码器容量对采样的影响（二元高斯玩具例子），d 为编码器最后一层线性映射的输入维度。当 d > n 和 d = n 时，三个数据点的样本都准确覆盖了各自的真实后验（GT）；一旦 d < n，中间那个数据点的样本塌缩成了一个点，直接印证了 Theorem 1 里 d ≥ n 的秩条件。

zh.text: 证据一：ALD 能采到 VI 采不到的后验
灵活性到底体现在哪？论文用一个“神经似然”玩具例子来看：让似然由一个随机初始化的神经网络定义，人为造出一个既多峰、又强相关的复杂后验，然后比较不同方法能否还原它。这类形状正是高斯替身分布的软肋。

zh.caption: 图3 神经似然例子中的后验对比。从左到右依次是真实后验（GT）、均场变分推断（Mean-field VI）、全变分推断（Full VI）和本文 ALD 的样本。均场 VI 只能覆盖单个峰，全 VI 也只能拟合一个带相关性的椭圆，而 ALD 的样本几乎复现了真实后验的多峰、弯曲结构。

zh.text: 结论很直接：均场 VI 把整个后验压成了一个孤立的峰，全 VI 稍好但也只是一个倾斜的椭圆，两者都丢掉了后验真实的多峰和弯曲结构；ALD 的样本则贴合了真实后验的形状。这说明把采样换成真正的 MCMC，确实带回了变分族拿不到的表达能力。
证据二：更准的后验，换来更好的生成模型
玩具例子说明 ALD 采得准，但训练深度生成模型时这份“准”值不值？论文在 MNIST、SVHN、CIFAR-10、CelebA 四个标准数据集上做了图像生成实验。为了公平，所有方法都用同样的全连接网络，用每维负 ELBO（negative evidence lower bound，越低越好）在三个随机种子上评测。

zh.caption: 表1 四个数据集上的图像生成结果，指标为每维负 ELBO（三个种子的均值，越低越好）。LAE 在全部四个数据集上都取得了最低值，稳定优于 VAE、VAE-flow 和 Hoffman [2017]。

zh.text: 四个数据集上 LAE 都拿到了最低的负 ELBO：MNIST 从 VAE 的 1.189 降到 1.177，CIFAR-10 从 4.820 降到 4.773，CelebA 从 4.671 降到 4.636，SVHN 从 4.442 降到 4.412。绝对提升不算大，但方向一致——更准的后验采样确实转化成了更好训练的生成模型。代价是训练时间：LAE 大约比 VAE 慢 2.24 倍，不过和同样带采样的 Hoffman [2017] 基本持平。而且这些结果只用了 T = 2 步 ALD 迭代。
什么在起作用：MH 步和迭代次数 T
既然 T = 2 就够了，那 T 到底重不重要？MH 拒绝步又值不值得加？论文在 MNIST 上画出了测试集负 ELBO 的学习曲线来回答。

zh.caption: 图4 MNIST 测试集负 ELBO 的学习曲线。T = 2 与 T = 10 两条曲线几乎重合，说明只要迭代步数不小于 2，增加 T 对性能几乎没有影响；而去掉 MH 拒绝步（No MH steps）后曲线剧烈震荡，说明 MH 步对稳定训练很关键。

zh.text: 两个观察很清楚。其一，T = 2 和 T = 10 的曲线基本贴在一起，说明只要 ALD 迭代不少于 2 步，再增加步数收益微乎其微——这也是为什么图像实验只用 T = 2。其二，一旦拿掉 MH 拒绝步，曲线开始大幅上下抖动，训练明显不稳定；MH 步虽然要额外算一点，却是把训练稳住的关键。配合前面的图2，这两个消融从理论条件（d ≥ n）和工程细节（MH、T）两头把方法的行为交代清楚了。
小结：把自编码器重新理解为一种有偏差修正的采样器
这篇工作最优雅的地方，是它对“随机性放在哪里”的重新安排。把 Langevin 噪声从隐变量搬到编码器参数上，采样一下子既高效（因为在所有数据上摊销），又灵活（因为它是货真价实的 MCMC，而不是被约束的高斯）。由此得到的 LAE 在理论上是一个合法的 MCMC 方法，在代码上几乎就是一个标准自编码器，却能在测试似然上稳定超过 VAE。
换个角度看，它其实是把我们熟悉的自编码器，重新解释成了变分推断的一个“采样版、带偏差修正”的替代方案。当然，边界也要说清楚：它的收敛保证依赖“固定特征提取器 + 可训练线性末层，且 d ≥ n”这样的编码器结构，实验也集中在全连接网络和这几个标准数据集上，绝对提升幅度温和，并且要付出约 2.24 倍的训练时间。它更像是打开了一扇门——让 MCMC 第一次真正被摊销进深度生成模型的训练里。

en.text: The method: let the Langevin noise act on the encoder's parameters

The key move in ALD is to change what the randomness acts on. Traditional Langevin runs a stochastic differential equation (SDE) on each latent z; ALD instead defines a deterministic encoder f(x; φ) that maps observations to latents, and runs the Langevin equation on the encoder's parameters φ. Because the latents are produced by the encoder, dynamics on φ induce dynamics on the latent space — so the encoder's outputs can be read off directly as posterior samples.

Written out, the update on the parameters is dφ = −∇φ V(φ) dt + √2 dB, where the potential V(φ) = Σ U(x⁽ⁱ⁾, f(x⁽ⁱ⁾; φ); θ) sums the negative log-joint over all data points. Discretized, each step is a draw from a Gaussian: φ′ ~ N(φ − η∇φV(φ), 2ηI). The important detail is that every data point shares the same parameters φ, so a single update advances the sampling for all of them at once — which is exactly what amortization means here.

Moving the noise onto the parameters isn't free, though: you need a guarantee that the latents you read off are actually distributed according to the posterior you wanted. The paper's Theorem 1 supplies the condition. When the encoder has the form f(x; Φ) = Φ g(x) — a fixed feature extractor g followed by a trainable last linear layer Φ — and the width d of that layer is at least the number of data points n in the batch, the latent samples induced by ALD converge to the true posterior. Two clean special cases fall out: traditional Langevin dynamics is a special case of ALD, and the ordinary autoencoder is a special case of the LAE.

The Langevin Autoencoder simply folds this sampler into the training loop. Before each decoder update, it runs T ALD steps on the encoder's last layer to draw posterior samples, optionally followed by a Metropolis-Hastings (MH) rejection step that removes the bias introduced by discretization. In code it looks almost identical to a standard autoencoder — the only difference is that the encoder takes a few noisy update steps along the way.
That d ≥ n condition is not just theory. In a bivariate-Gaussian toy problem, the authors vary the input dimensionality d of the encoder's last layer and watch what happens to the samples.

zh.text: 方法：让 Langevin 噪声作用在编码器参数上
ALD 的关键一步，是换一个施加随机性的对象。传统 Langevin 把随机微分方程（SDE）跑在每个隐变量 z 上；ALD 则定义一个确定性的编码器 f(x; φ)，把数据映射到隐变量，然后把 Langevin 方程跑在编码器的参数 φ 上。因为隐变量是编码器算出来的，参数 φ 的动力学就会诱导出隐变量空间上的动力学，于是可以直接把编码器的输出当作后验样本。
参数上的 Langevin 更新写出来是这样：dφ = −∇φ V(φ) dt + √2 dB，其中势能 V(φ) = Σ U(x⁽ⁱ⁾, f(x⁽ⁱ⁾; φ); θ) 把所有数据点的负对数联合概率加在一起。离散化后每一步就是从一个高斯里采样：φ′ ~ N(φ − η∇φV(φ), 2ηI)。注意这里所有数据点共享同一组参数 φ，一次更新就同时推进了全部数据点的采样——这正是“摊销”的含义。

但把噪声搬到参数上不会白搬，需要一个保证：这样采出来的隐变量，真的服从我们想要的后验吗？论文的 Theorem 1 给出了条件。当编码器写成 f(x; Φ) = Φ g(x)，即一个固定的特征提取器 g 后面接一个可训练的最后一层线性映射 Φ，并且这个线性层的维度 d 不小于当前 batch 的数据点数 n 时，ALD 诱导出的隐变量样本会收敛到真实后验。两个漂亮的特例随之而来：传统 Langevin 动力学是 ALD 的特例，而普通的自编码器则是 LAE 的特例。
Langevin 自编码器（LAE）就是把这套采样直接嵌进训练循环：每次更新解码器参数之前，先在编码器最后一层上跑 T 步 ALD 得到后验样本，可选地再加一个 Metropolis-Hastings（MH）拒绝步来消除离散化带来的偏差。从代码上看，它和一个标准自编码器几乎一模一样，区别只是编码器多走了几步带噪声的更新。

The first camp is variational inference (VI) — the machinery behind the VAE. This NeurIPS 2022 paper from the University of Tokyo asks whether you can have both — the amortized efficiency of VI and the sampling flexibility of MCMC. Its answer is the Langevin Autoencoder (LAE), built on a new sampling algorithm the authors call Amortized Langevin Dynamics (ALD). The one-line intuition: take the noise that Langevin sampling injects into the latent variables, and move it onto the encoder's parameters instead.

zh.caption: 图4 MNIST 测试集负 ELBO 的学习曲线。T = 2 与 T = 10 两条曲线几乎重合，说明只要迭代步数不小于 2，增加 T 对性能几乎没有影响；而去掉 MH 拒绝步（No MH steps）后曲线剧烈震荡，说明 MH 步对稳定训练很关键。
